name: Theodora
info: Theodora (c. 495–548), a bear keeper's daughter and former actress, was the wife of Justinian I and Eastern Roman empress from 527, one of his chief political advisers and a protector of the Miaphysite Christians.

facts.born: c. 490/500, most likely around 495 and probably in Constantinople (later sources name Syria, Cyprus, Paphlagonia or Alexandria); daughter of Acacius, bear keeper for the Green faction of the Hippodrome, and of a dancer and actress whose name was not recorded
facts.died: 28 June 548, of a disease that Victor of Tunnuna records in Greek terms usually translated as "cancer"; buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople
facts.role: Wife of Justinian I; Eastern Roman empress (augusta) from 527 to 548 and one of the emperor's chief political advisers
facts.known: her stand during the Nika riots of 532, as Procopius tells it; the closing of the brothels and the Metanoia convent for former prostitutes; sheltering Miaphysite leaders and monks; the fall of John the Cappadocian and of Pope Silverius; the mosaic of San Vitale in Ravenna; the hostile portrait in Procopius's Secret History

t: Born to a bear keeper of the Hippodrome and working as an actress in her youth, Theodora married Justinian after a law of 524 allowed senators to marry actresses, and was crowned empress in 527.

As empress she advised Justinian, steadied the court during the Nika riots by Procopius's account, closed brothels, sheltered persecuted Miaphysites against her husband's Chalcedonian policy, and plotted the fall of rivals such as John the Cappadocian.
Most of what is known of her comes from Procopius, who praised her in public and slandered her in his Secret History, and historians remain divided over how far to believe him.
dyk: Theodora sheltered so many persecuted Miaphysite monks in the palace that on one occasion several hundred gathered in a grand chamber and the floor collapsed.
ev: Born, most likely in Constantinople, the daughter of Acacius, a bear keeper for the Green faction
After the death of Empress Euphemia, Justin issues an edict allowing actresses to marry senators, opening the way to her marriage with Justinian
Crowned augusta when Justinian succeeds to the throne
With Justinian orders the closing of the brothels and the arrest of their keepers
During the Nika riots, by Procopius's account, speaks against flight in the emperor's council
With Antonina, wife of Belisarius, brings about the fall of the praetorian prefect John the Cappadocian
The mosaics of San Vitale in Ravenna, showing her in full imperial dress, are completed
Dies and is buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople

sections.early:
Much of Theodora's early life is uncertain, including the date and place of her birth; the modern consensus is that she was born around 495 and raised in Constantinople, though later sources placed her birth in Syria, Cyprus, Paphlagonia or Alexandria. Her father, Acacius, was a bear keeper for the Green faction of the Hippodrome, and her mother, whose name was not recorded, was a dancer and actress. She had an elder sister, Comito, and a younger, Anastasia. After her father died, the Greens gave her stepfather's post to someone else for a bribe; her mother brought the children before the crowd as suppliants, and when the Greens refused them the Blue faction gave the family the position.

The foremost source for her youth is Procopius's Secret History, which some modern scholars regard as often unreliable and slanderous. According to it she worked as an actress before adolescence, and acting then included indecent shows on stage and sexual services off it; John of Ephesus also says she came "from the brothel". David Potter judges that beneath Procopius's inventions "there lies the semblance of fact". She later went to North Africa as the concubine of Hecebolus, governor of the Libyan Pentapolis, and after they parted travelled to Alexandria and Antioch. Some historians speculate that she became a Miaphysite in Alexandria, but there is no reliable evidence of it.
sections.rise:
Theodora returned to Constantinople and met Justinian, likely sometime before 524. He wished to marry her, but a law from the time of Constantine barred men of senatorial rank from marrying actresses, and Justin's wife, Empress Euphemia, strongly opposed the match. After Euphemia died in 524, Justin issued an edict that same year allowing actresses to marry senators, and the couple married. The same law excused the children of former actresses, so Theodora's illegitimate daughter could marry a relative of the late emperor Anastasius; a great-granddaughter through this line married Peter, brother of the emperor Maurice. A story that she made a son named Ioannes disappear is doubted by James Allan Evans, since she openly acknowledged her daughter.

When Justinian succeeded to the throne in 527, Theodora was crowned augusta. According to the Secret History she took part in state councils and had great influence over her husband. In Novel 8.1 of 535, a law against corruption under which provincial officials swore an oath to the emperor and to Theodora, Justinian called her his "partner in my deliberations". Procopius, confirmed by the poet Corippus, says the couple changed the court ceremonies so that officials kissed the feet of both, and required to be called "master" and "mistress".
sections.deeds:
In January 532 the Blue and Green factions, united against the emperor, rioted under the cry "Nika", burned public buildings and proclaimed Hypatius, nephew of Anastasius I, emperor. According to Procopius, as Justinian and his officials prepared to flee, Theodora spoke in the council against flight, saying that for one who has reigned it is intolerable to be a fugitive and that "royal purple" is the noblest shroud. Justinian's troops attacked the crowd in the Hippodrome, killing over 30,000, and Hypatius and his brother Pompeius were put to death, in one source at her insistence. J. A. S. Evans notes that the speech echoes advice once given to the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse and suggests Procopius dramatised the scene.

Theodora and Justinian commissioned many buildings in Constantinople, the most famous Hagia Sophia, and she was involved in the Church of Sergius and Bacchus, whose inscription praises her care for the destitute. In 528 the couple ordered the brothels closed and their keepers and procurers arrested; she paid the owners the purchase price of the women, freed them and gave each clothing and a gold nomisma. She founded the Metanoia convent on the Asian side of the Dardanelles, where former prostitutes could support themselves, and she compelled the general Artabanes to take back the wife he had abandoned. She also arranged marriages that bound her family to the old nobility, among them her niece Sophia's to Justinian's nephew Justin II.
sections.opponents:
Theodora was reputed to be a Miaphysite and worked against her husband's support of the Chalcedonian church, and pro-Chalcedonians accused her of fostering heresy; Procopius and Evagrius Scholasticus, followed by some modern historians, suggested the couple only pretended to disagree. She sheltered Miaphysite leaders such as Severus and Anthimus, whom she had helped to become Patriarch of Constantinople and hid in her quarters for ten years after his excommunication. When Pope Silverius refused to lift the anathema on Anthimus, she had Belisarius find a pretext to remove him; Silverius was exiled to a rocky island, where he starved to death, and Vigilius took his place. Among the Nobatae, south of Egypt, she had the Duke of Thebaid delay her husband's Chalcedonian missionaries so that hers arrived first.

Sources generally describe her as vindictive but determined and loyal, and also as cruel and inspiring fear. Procopius alleges that she ordered the murder of the Ostrogothic queen Amalasuintha, which a surviving letter from King Theodahad independently supports. His Secret History, written after her death, portrays her as shameless, cruel and lustful: it claims she "rounded up" 500 prostitutes and confined them in the convent, where some leapt the walls to escape, whereas John Malalas wrote that she freed the girls from the yoke of their wretched slavery. Procopius also accused her of unfairly championing wives charged with adultery.
sections.last:
Theodora remained active at court in her last years. She was at odds with the praetorian prefect John the Cappadocian, a close ally of the emperor whom she resented for his influence, his wealth and his slanders of her. In 541 she and Antonina, the wife of Belisarius, laid a trap: Antonina led John's daughter to believe in a plot to put Belisarius on the throne, John was caught making treasonous remarks, and he was removed. She was also hostile to Justinian's cousin Germanus, while the prefect Peter Barsymes was her ally. According to the Secret History she pressed for her grandson Anastasius to marry Joannina, the daughter and heiress of Belisarius and Antonina, against the parents' will, and the couple eventually married.

The mosaics of the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna, completed in 547, show her in full imperial dress with a communion chalice. She died on 28 June 548. Victor of Tunnuna records the death in Greek terms usually translated as "cancer", probably meaning a suppurating ulcer or malignant tumour; later accounts call it breast cancer, which the original report does not say. She was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles, and in a procession in 559 Justinian visited her tomb and lit candles in her memory. Her niece Sophia later became empress beside Justin II.
sections.legacy:
Theodora is recognised as a saint in the Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox Churches and commemorated on 14 November. The Miaphysites, who regard her as one of their own, believed her influence over Justinian was so strong that after her death he worked for harmony between them and the Chalcedonians and kept his promise to protect her community of Miaphysite refugees in the Hormisdas Palace; she had given much political support to the ministry of Jacob Baradaeus. Olbia in Cyrenaica, now Qasr Libya, was renamed Theodorias after her, and Cululis in Africa Proconsularis Theodoriana. According to one historian, "No empress left so profound a mark on the imagination of her people as did Theodora." Plays, operas, films and novels have been written about her.

Her reputation rests largely on Procopius, who praised her courage in the Wars, slandered her in the Secret History, published only in 1623, and flattered her piety in the Buildings. James Allan Evans holds that the hostile portrait shows how the upper classes felt threatened by her power, Averil Cameron that its demons were a contemporary way to rationalise the inexplicable, and Peter Heather calls it arguably the most effective character assassination ever written. Anthony Kaldellis and Clive Foss answer that independent sources confirm her theatre background, the marriage law and her ruthlessness, and Foss thinks Procopius embellished rather than invented.

summary: Theodora rose from the theatre of Constantinople to marry Justinian I and rule beside him as empress from 527 to 548. She advised him, closed brothels, sheltered Miaphysites against his church policy and removed rivals by intrigue, and nearly everything told of her passes through Procopius, whose praise and slander historians still weigh against other sources.

notes: Birth: the lead gives c. 490/500, the Early years section a consensus of about 495; start set to 495 with circa true.
The article gives no place of death; facts and events say only where she was buried.
Nika speech quoted only in part, as Procopius gives it; the article itself says it may represent palace discussions rather than her literal words.

Left out: the doubted story of the son Ioannes beyond one line; the Daman birthplace and priest's-daughter tradition of the later Miaphysite sources (Bar-Hebraeus, Michael the Syrian), for want of room.
